newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Official Russian crop forecasts seen too high.
newsitem.headline: Official Russian crop forecasts seen too high.

text.p: Russia could be facing another dismal grain harvest this year, but government officials are keeping quiet about their own and others' lower forecasts, industry sources said on Monday.

Anatoly Altukhov, a senior specialist at the Scientific Research Centre for Agricultural Economics, Labour and Management, said the cabinet and Agriculture Ministry had privately lowered their forecasts to about 73 million tonnes from 75-77 million.
"Almost everybody is now talking about 10 million tonnes above last year," Altukhov said, referring to 1995's official output of 63.4 million tonnes, the worst in three decades.
A spokesman for First Deputy Prime Alexander Zaveryukha said the minister, who is in charge of the harvest, had not publicly changed his forecast.
The harvest is a sensitive issue, and ministry and cabinet officials do not like to discuss crop problems or failures.
The Centre for Economic Trends said it had revised its net grain harvest forecast down to 68 million tonnes, lopping one million tonnes off its previous estimate earlier this month.

"Forty percent of the harvest remains to be brought in," said Maria Goncharyova, head of the centre's food supplies section, referring to concerns over losses due to drought, rains and slow reaping as winter nears in some regions.
The centre forecast average wheat yields at 1.29 tonnes per hectare, well below the 1.6 tonnes estimated by the State Statistics Committee.

"A huge amount of food wheat has been lost and will be used only as feed," said Vladimir Totsky, vice-president of the Grain Union, a private organisation grouping traders and some producers. "This is not just very bad, it's a catastrophe."
He said that only 7-10 percent of all the food wheat planted in Rostov, a large grain-growing region, was suitable for bread.
The amount of grain usable for food was 18 percent, 30 percent and 45 percent respectively of the total sown to bread wheat in the Volga, Krasnodar and Stavropol regions.

"There are lots of rumours about imports in connection with the bad wheat harvest, and it's possible there will be some hard wheat and maize (corn) buying," Totsky said. The union was not making its own forecasts of net output.
"But nobody knows by whom, when, or if this will actually happen," he said, adding that cash resources for buying were even tighter this year at state and private organisations.

Interfax news agency said farmers were offering more feed grains, including maize, for sale to other areas, but Totsky said Rostov and Stavropol regions had temporarily banned sales until regional reserves were filled to meet demand.
Goncharyova said Russia had sown 2.7 million fewer hectares this year and three million ha had been lost to drought. --Moscow Newsroom, +7095 941 8520
